t: Introduction: the histological method and its forensic medical place
n: In this lecture we will consider the forensic medical place of the histological method. Microscopy allows post-mortem degradation of bone to be assessed at the level of microstructure. In skin injuries, immunohistochemistry, IHC, along with biochemistry and molecular biology is among the methods most often used in studying the age of an injury. In bone, thin sections are stained, and then the collagen and osteocytes, which undergo taphonomic change, that is change under the influence of the post-mortem environment, become visible. In the review on bone, 45 promising stains were identified, but in taphonomic studies only 3 of them were tested.

t: Forensic medical tasks of the histological method
n: The forensic medical tasks of the histological method differ according to the object. In skin, it is first important to establish whether the injury was formed during life, that is its vitality. For this, IHC and immunofluorescence, IF, are used. If vitality is confirmed, the time after injury, PTI, substantiates the link between trauma and death. In bone, however, the method consists of staining a thin section. There, the changes may be related to the post-mortem interval, PMI, or the burial interval, BI.

t: The problem of assessing injury age and the advantage of IHC
n: Assessment of injury age is an important problem in forensic pathology: no gold standard system has been proposed, and it remains difficult to determine the time exactly. There is much evidence in the literature on IHC. A wide choice of markers, that is tissue molecules, cytokines and growth factors, helps to determine vitality. IHC is convenient, reliable and, unlike other methods, can analyse the location, that is the localisation, of the molecules needed. Attention: the results of IHC are sometimes contradictory. Therefore, not a single marker but a panel of markers may be more reliable in determining injury age.

t: Vitality and PTI: why they matter
n: We consider why vitality and PTI matter. A vital injury is formed during life; the main task is to distinguish it from post-mortem skin change. The chain is as follows: a skin injury is identified, vitality is checked, that is an answer is obtained to the question whether it was during life, then PTI is assessed and a causal relationship between the injury and death is established. After vitality is confirmed, the interval after injury, PTI, is assessed. Attention: vitality and PTI are not the same. A gold standard for assessing injury age has not yet been proposed.

t: Review methodology: search and PRISMA
n: Review methodology and PRISMA. The search began on 18 February 2023: PubMed and Scopus, articles from 1973–2022. Immunohistochemistry, IHC, and immunofluorescence, IF, were studied; the PRISMA reporting rules formed the basis. First 326 articles were found, they were screened by criteria, 29 articles were taken, and with additions from the bibliography the total came to 46 articles. The articles were assessed independently by three researchers; disagreements were resolved by consensus.

t: Inclusion and exclusion criteria
n: Inclusion and exclusion criteria. Included: full text in English, original, prospective and retrospective cohort studies, determination of PTI using IHC and IF. As samples, corpse skin, biopsy of a living person, and mouse, rat and pig skin were taken. Excluded: articles not in English, reviews and systematic reviews, methods other than IHC, and tissues other than skin. That is, the review is directed only at skin and only at immunological methods.

t: Results: article screening and share of methods
n: Results: article screening and share of methods. Of 326 articles, PubMed 288, Scopus 38, 29 were included; with additions from the lists the total came to 46. The shares of methods are as follows: IHC alone 32, that is 70 %, IF alone 5, that is 10 %, IHC and IF together 9, that is 20 %. In 25 studies a multi-marker approach was used, in 21 a single-marker approach. In 31 studies there was statistical analysis, and in 15 only qualitative observations were given.

t: Case analysis 1: screening of articles
n: The first case analysis: screening of articles. Situation: researchers found 326 articles on assessing injury age in the PubMed and Scopus databases. Excluded: 19 not in English, 14 reviews, 235 with another method or another tissue, 29 duplicates. Calculation: 19+14+235+29 = 297 excluded, and the remaining 29 articles were included in the analysis. Question: why was it necessary to screen by precisely these criteria, that is language, type of article, method and tissue?

t: Quick question 1
n: The first quick questions. Question 1: what is PTI? Answer: post-trauma interval, that is the time that has passed since the injury was formed. Question 2: why is PTI important? Answer: it helps to establish the causal link between the injury and death. Question 3: what is the main advantage of IHC? Answer: it is easy to use, reliable, and can analyse the location of molecules. Attention: IHC and IF follow the state and progress of the injury, but cannot determine the time of death, that is the post-mortem interval, exactly.

t: Stages of wound healing
n: Stages of wound healing. The healing process begins immediately with the appearance of the injury; first bleeding is stopped, this is haemostasis. Then inflammation, migration and multiplication of cells, that is proliferation and migration, and formation of new vessels, angiogenesis, continue. At the end the epithelium covers the injury, this is re-epithelialisation, and collagen is synthesised and gives the tissue strength.

t: Coagulation factors: the first hours
n: Coagulation factors and the first hours. Van de Goot constructed a scoring system for assessing injury age on the basis of fibronectin, CD62p and factor VIII. In fresh injuries the immunohistochemistry, IHC, score of all three markers was higher than in healthy control skin, difference p < 0.001. These markers stain positive in early injury, especially at an interval after injury, PTI, of 0–1 hour.

t: FVIIIra, CD15 and tryptase: sensitivity and specificity
n: FVIIIra, CD15 and tryptase: sensitivity and specificity. Gauchotte studied the time of punctured skin injuries with the markers FVIIIra, CD15 and tryptase. The sensitivity of FVIIIra is 100 %, but the specificity 47 %. It was also raised in surgical and control injuries, 53 %, so the specificity is low. CD15 and tryptase, however, distinguish fresh ante-mortem from post-mortem, that is they are more useful markers. Attention: sensitivity and specificity are not the same; high sensitivity does not yet make a marker reliable.

t: Attention: sensitivity ≠ specificity
n: Attention: the difference between sensitivity and specificity. Gauchotte and colleagues tested the marker FVIIIra. Its sensitivity was 100%, and the specificity only 47%. The rise of FVIIIra was also seen in surgical and negative control injuries, 53%. That is, the marker is not specific to a vital injury. Therefore FVIIIra is regarded as a highly sensitive but non-specific marker of the vitality of an injury. For distinguishing a recent vital injury from a post-mortem one, CD15 and tryptase are regarded as more useful.

t: Time peaks of inflammatory cytokines
n: Time peaks of inflammatory cytokines. Kondo, 1996: a statistically significant peak of TNFα and IL-1β was found 3 hours after injury. A smaller but significant peak of IL-1β was seen at 6 hours, and the peak of IL-6 at 12 hours. Neutrophils at 3–6 hours, and phagocytes at 24 hours, that is in the transitional phase, stained positive for these cytokines.

t: IL-1α, IL-8, MCP-1 and MIP-1α
n: IL-1α, IL-8, MCP-1 and MIP-1α. Kondo, 1999: neutrophils appeared 4 hours after injury. Their cytoplasm stained with anti-IL-1α and remained positive up to a day. If the proportion of IL-1α-positive cells exceeds 30%, the age of the injury may be a day or less. Grellner: IL-1, IL-6 and TNF-α appear early in a vital injury; the earliest response was seen at 15 minutes and persisted for several hours. Kondo, 2002: IL-8, MCP-1, that is monocyte chemoattractant protein, and MIP-1α were first found in neutrophils up to 12 hours, then in macrophages and fibroblasts.

t: Immune cells: neutrophil, macrophage, lymphocyte
n: Immune cells: neutrophil, macrophage and lymphocyte. Fronczek studied skin biopsies of living people: immune cells give a time-dependent pattern according to the age of injury. Neutrophils and MIP-1-positive inflammatory cells are markedly more numerous in injuries 0.2–4 days old. Active macrophages, CD68, peak at 2–4 days. Lymphocytes, CD45, peak at 0.2–2 days, then fall up to 10 days. Attention: IL-8 expression in the epidermis is not related to the age of injury.

t: CD14 and dendritic cells
n: CD14 and dendritic cells. Yagi: CD14 rises markedly 2–5 days after injury. In identifying an injury 1–5 days old, sensitivity is 100% and specificity 87.2%. If CD14, CD32B and CD68 are all three positive, the injury is 1–5 days old; if all three are negative, it is assessed as younger than one day. Fouad: the peak of CD14 is at 1–3 days, 96.40 ± 3.78%, and after 3 days falls sharply, 14.80 ± 3.49%. Attention: the intervals of Yagi and Fouad differ. Kuninaka: if the number of CD11c+/HLA-DRα+ dendritic cells exceeds 50, the age of the injury is 4–14 days. With other markers the interval is narrowed.

t: Mast cells, histamine and VCAM-1
n: Mast cells, histamine and VCAM-1. Bonelli: in a vital injury the number of mast cells peaks at 1–3 hours; in post-mortem cases they are markedly fewer. Jebur: mast cell density in the dermis is higher than in controls and is directly related to the time elapsed since injury. Zhong and Zhen: in human and rat skin the amount of histamine rises gradually after injury up to 30 minutes. Dressler: expression of VCAM-1, that is vascular cell adhesion molecule-1, peaks at 4–6 hours, then falls. By itself it is insufficient for assessing injury age.

t: Case analysis 2: cytokine and immune markers
n: The second case analysis: cytokine and immune markers. Situation: in the biopsy CD14 is high and the trio CD14/CD32B/CD68 is positive. In Yagi's study CD14 rose markedly 2–5 days after injury. If the trio is positive, the age of injury is 1–5 days; if negative, it was assessed as less than 1 day. Fouad: the peak of CD14 is at 1–3 days, 96.40 ± 3.78%, and after 3 days it fell sharply, 14.80 ± 3.49%. Approximate age: 1–3 days. Why is one marker not enough? VCAM-1 alone is insufficient for an exact age. A panel of markers is more reliable than a single marker.

t: Quick question 2
n: The second quick questions. Question 1: which markers are positive early, at 0–1 hour? Answer: fibronectin, CD62p, factor VIII and FVIIIra, CD15, tryptase. Question 2: which cytokines have a 3-hour peak? Answer: TNFα and IL-1β; the IL-6 peak is 12 hours after injury. Question 3: which indicator points to a later 4–14 days? Answer: the number of dendritic cells >50, CD11c+/HLA-DRα+. Attention, risk of error: FVIIIra has sensitivity 100% and specificity 47%; sensitivity and specificity are not the same, and it is never sole evidence.

t: Growth factors: TGF and VEGF
n: Growth factors: TGF and VEGF. TGF-α and TGF-β1 respond at 10 minutes and are sharply intensified at 30–60 minutes. TGF-α is similar to EGF and regulates early angiogenesis; TGF-α and TGF-β1 are not related to each other. VEGF-negative neutrophils are seen from 4 hours to 1 day. If VEGF-positive cells are >50%, the age of injury may be 7–14 days. In the rat the peak was seen at 5–7 days.

t: Enzymes: esterase, MMP, COX-2
n: Enzymes: esterase, MMP and COX-2. Non-specific esterase was found in about 40% of vital injuries, in the interval from 1 hour to 5 days. MMP-2+ macrophages at >25 cells point to 9–12 days, and MMP-9+ macrophages at >30 cells to 3–14 days. MMP-2+ and MMP-9+ macrophages increase with the age of the wound; the MMP-9 interval in the source is given as 4–14 and 3–14 days. Attention: COX-2, that is cyclooxygenase-2, at >40% is 8 hours–3 days; >50% may be forensically significant.

t: Collagens and the basement membrane timeline
n: Collagens and the basement membrane timeline. Collagen III is not visible before 2.5 days and intensifies at >5 days. Collagen V appears on the third day and is weaker than III. Collagens I and VI appear at about 6–7 days; their absence indicates that the wound is younger than 6–7 days. Attention: type VII is the basement membrane collagen; its fragments are seen at about 4 days, and full reorganisation at 8+ days.

t: Myofibroblast, laminin, fibronectin, tenascin, selectin
n: Myofibroblast, laminin, fibronectin, tenascin and selectin. α-SMA, that is alpha smooth muscle actin, positive myofibroblasts appear at about 5 days; they indicate a wound about 5 days old or older, and do not define an old wound exactly. Laminin and HSPG around the myofibroblast indicate a wound at least 1.5 days old; laminin is more useful because it is found in more cells and in the wound. Attention: fibronectin has been studied as a sign of vitality, but a post-mortem positive reaction may be due to transudation of blood components. Tenascin staining weakens with the age of the wound and is still visible at about 1.5 months; E-selectin is found from 1 hour to 17 days, and falls markedly at 12 hours.

t: Other markers: AQP, ORP150, ubiquitin, CHI3L1, EPC
n: Other markers: AQP, ORP150, ubiquitin, CHI3L1 and EPC. Aquaporins, AQP, are water channel proteins that take part in cell migration. If the number of AQP3-positive cells is >300, this points to 5–10 days. ORP150 is a protein that rises in cell stress; a positive proportion >50% means 7–14 days. EPC, that is endothelial progenitor cells, appear from day 2 and increase. CHI3L1 rises sharply at days 4–6. Ubiquitin: at an early stage a strong positive reaction is seen in neutrophils and inside the nucleus.

t: Time map by marker groups
n: Time map by marker groups. Coagulation factors, that is fibronectin, CD62p and factor VIII, are most clearly positive at 0–1 hour, in the first hour. Cytokine and immune markers, from 1 hour to 5 days, for example IL-1, TNFα, CD14 and macrophages. Dendritic cells >50, up to 14 days. Other markers, that is AQP, ORP150, ubiquitin and EPC, indicate 2–14 days. Attention: a single marker is unreliable; a multi-marker panel is regarded as the most reliable approach.

t: Case analysis 3: enzymes and collagens
n: The third case analysis: enzymes and collagens. Situation: in the injury sample, the proportion of cells positive for cyclooxygenase-2, COX-2, is >40%, and collagens I and VI were not found. A COX-2 proportion >40% shows an injury age of 8 hours to 3 days; >50% may be forensically significant. Collagens I and VI usually appear on days 6–7; their absence means the injury age is less than 6–7 days. Conclusion: the two results do not contradict each other, and the injury is in the approximate interval of 8 hours–3 days. Question: which additional marker will refine this?

t: Summary of the skin section: the multi-marker approach
n: Summary of the skin section: the multi-marker approach. When several markers and methods are used together, sensitivity and specificity are high, but the work requires more time and complexity. A panel of markers is more reliable than a single marker. The multi-marker approach is regarded as the most reliable way of assessing injury age. Attention: immunohistochemistry, IHC, and immunofluorescence, IF, follow the progress and vitality of the injury but cannot determine the post-mortem interval exactly. In future, new studies are needed to find a highly sensitive and specific marker for assessing injury age after death.

t: Bone histology: diagenesis and the taphonomic environment
n: Bone histology: diagenesis and the taphonomic environment. Diagenesis is the chemical and physical change of bone: the ratio of collagen to hydroxyapatite shifts. Decomposition of the corpse proceeds under the influence of the atmosphere, lithosphere and biosphere; temperature, humidity, pH and microbes play a part. As a result the ratio of organic to inorganic changes, and a possibility of linkage with PMI and BI appears. If temperature rises by 10 °C, the reaction rate, including microbial activity, doubles. Attention: the post-mortem interval, PMI, and burial interval, BI, are assessed depending on the environment.

t: Bone PMI studies: a review of 13 articles
n: Bone PMI studies: a review of 13 articles. A systematic search was carried out in PubMed and ScienceDirect for 1980–2023, English-language articles only; decomposition in a water environment was excluded. In the final 13 articles, three studies used Sirius Red/Fast Green, two haematoxylin and eosin, H&E, and one Picrosirius Red. In all studies embedded bone was used; in Delannoy, 2018, and Astolphi, 2019, the bone was decalcified. In the studies of Boaks, 2014, and Jellinghaus, 2018 and 2019, non-decalcified bone was used.

t: Bone structure, autolysis and putrefaction
n: Bone structure, autolysis and putrefaction. Bone consists of about 20% spongy and about 80% dense substance. Composition: organic part 25%, inorganic 60–70%, water 9.7%. The organic part is mainly type I collagen. In autolysis, enzymes, that is protease and DNase, break down bone cells. Extracellular proteins such as collagen are resistant to autolysis. In putrefaction, acid metabolites partly dissolve the matrix. Micro-organisms penetrate inside and hydrolyse collagen with the help of collagenases. According to Hackett, the types of tunnelling are: Wedl, fungal, linear longitudinal, budding and laminar, the last three being bacterial.

t: Effect of acid and alkali on bone
n: The effect of acid and alkali on bone. In a strong acid, for example hydrochloric acid, HCl, bone dissolves within hours; cortical bone is more resistant. In 10% HCl the histological structure is affected in 19 hours, and in 37% HCl it is completely destroyed in 3 hours. Sulphuric acid dissolves bone in 7 days; and in 1 day integrity is lost. An alkali, lye, dissolves only the contents of the marrow cavity, and the structure is preserved. That is, acid acts on the minerals and alkali on the marrow cavity; the action of acid is similar to decalcification.

t: 45 stains and the gap in protocols
n: Now about the 45 stains and the gap in protocols. Collagen and osteocytes are shown by the methods of Mallory, Gomori trichrome and Weigert resorcin-fuchsin. In a non-decalcified section the ratio of organic to inorganic parts can be assessed. There are 45 promising stains, 8 protocols for embedded bone and 2 for non-embedded. Tested stains 3, untested 42. The lack of protocols and the untested status of 42 stains determine the direction of further research.

t: Bone integrity index and choice of stain
n: Bone integrity index and choice of stain. The ratio of osteocyte nuclei to lacunae is called the bone integrity index; it shows the degree of preservation and may be linked to PMI. For osteocytes, Heidenhain and Gomori trichrome, toluidine blue and Azan trichrome are suitable; H&E showed reduction of chondrocytes in 28 days. For the matrix, that is collagen, Picrosirius Red, picrofuchsin and Sirius Red/Fast Green may be used. Astolphi, 2019: the burial interval and integrity index are inversely related, but loss of matrix was not related to the interval; there is no validated method.

t: Tested stains: Sirius Red/Fast Green, PSR, H&E
n: Tested stains: Sirius Red/Fast Green, PSR and H&E. Sirius Red/Fast Green helps to narrow the interval of time of death, PMI, in pig and human bone; it shows the change in collagen integrity. Picrosirius Red shows collagen breakdown and time-dependent change. H&E shows bone morphology and the integrity index, that is the ratio of osteocyte nuclei to cavities, but for now is unsuitable for PMI. There is not yet a model predicting an unknown PMI; it must adapt to soil and environmental conditions.

t: Case analysis 4 and quick question: bone histology
n: The fourth case analysis and quick question: bone histology. Situation: in a section of buried bone the ratio of osteocyte nuclei to lacunae is low. This means the bone is poorly preserved. The burial interval is inversely related to the bone integrity index: if the interval lengthens, the index falls. The index rests on the ratio of nuclei to lacunae. There is no validated method linking the index to PMI, that is the period after death. Soil chemistry and hydrology change the result. Quick question: why does a low index not give an exact time? Attention: degree of preservation is not PMI; it also depends on the conditions of burial.

t: Limitations, subjectivity and the prospect of artificial intelligence
n: Limitations, subjectivity and the prospect of artificial intelligence. Assessment of the microscopic picture is mainly subjective: it depends on the examiner's experience and interpretation. As a result interpretation may be variable. Compact and spongy bone respond differently to stain. Inorganic material stained in the cavities of spongy bone has altered the collagen ratio. Histological pictures are often assessed by the Hedges index or by the presence or absence of certain features. Several experts reduce subjectivity. In future, artificial intelligence, AI, tools such as Cellpose may recognise structures and calculate the ratio of organic to inorganic. This will reduce human error.

t: Overall conclusion: the potential of the histological method
n: Overall conclusion. In assessing the age of a skin injury, the multi-marker approach is the most reliable; it raises sensitivity and specificity, but requires more time and complexity. IHC and immunofluorescence are effective in following the progress of an injury and that it was formed during life; they cannot determine the post-mortem interval exactly. In bone, 45 stains are promising, but only 3 have been tested. Degradation of collagen and osteocytes may be an indicator of time, but there is no validated model. Next step: to test the remaining stains on sections of non-decalcified bone, combine them, and verify the method in different conditions for validation.
